newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Moscow banks see future in regions.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Moscow banks see future in regions.

text.p: Leading Moscow banks, seeing no more growth potential in the competitive capital, are racing to expand in the untapped markets of the Russian regions.
The sheer size of the regions means local banks do not fear the newcomers and local authorities and companies often prefer to deal with strong Moscow banks rather than weak regional institutions.

"Moscow is a very narrow market, it is a financial centre," Uneximbank deputy chairman Igor Antonov told Reuters. "The future is in the regions. Moscow will remain a financial centre, but real money will be earned outside Moscow."
Only four non-Moscow banks now make it into Rating agency's list of the top 30 Russians banks in terms of assets. Two of them are in St Petersburg banks.

Moscow was once the heart of the Russian economy, accounting for about 80 percent of the country's wealth, while the regions, crippled by a non-payments crisis and falling industrial output, remained on the fringes.
But the situation has changed, bankers said.
"The worst time for the regions is over. Take any big producer. They have separate divisions making competitive goods and you can grant them a credit," Antonov said.
REGIONS CAN OFFER BETTER RETURN
At the same time banks can earn a better return on funds in the regions than in Moscow, where competition has pushed down margins, bankers said.
Almost all the big Russian banks have a presence in St Petersburg, Nizhny Novgorod and Yektaterinburg. But now they are looking further afield.

Bank Rossiisky Kredit, one of the Moscow banks leading the thrust into the regions, believes the Urals and Siberia have the best prospects, said Dmitry Dorofeyev, head of planning in its regional expansion department.
The industrial production crisis will be over in these regions earlier than in others because of their competitive companies, he said.
The most interesting cities for the bank are Chelyabinsk and Yekaterinburg in the Urals, Vladivostok and Khabarovsk in the Far East and Krasnoyarsk in Siberia, he said.

"Expansion into the regions is now a priority for Rossiisky Kredit," Dorofeyev said. "Moscow is now oversupplied with banking services, while the regions have a huge growth potential which allows the bank to diversify risks."
Rossiisky Kredit opened 22 regional branches between 1993 and 1995, he said. This year it opened seven and plans to open seven more.
Inkombank, another leader in regional expansion, has 50 regional branches and has applied to open six more, a bank spokesman said.

Regional expansion is not a priority for Uneximbank, but it has opened three regional subsidiaries and branches in the last three years and plans to open three more in the next six months, Antonov said.
"If we want to compete successfully with other big Russian banks, we must be present on regional markets," he said.
Rossiisky Kredit's Dorofyeyev said there was still plenty of room in the regions for many banks.
"It is too early to speak about tough fighting for the regions," he said. "Regional markets for banking services are so capacious and so untapped that big banks can find a place."
Besides, only major banks can afford costly regional expansion. There are at most 20 such banks at present, he said.
Local bankers believe the regions can absorb many more banks, and do not fear expansion from Moscow.

"We are not afraid of Moscow banks' expansion, although we understand they have more money," said Yadviga Dobryanskaya, president of Bank Dalnevostochny in the Russian Far East. "The Far East region is developing very quickly. Everyone can find his place."
The attitude of local authorities to Moscow banks has changed crucially in the last few years, bankers said.
Municipalities prefer Moscow banks to open subsidiaries as they have to pay local taxes.

"They used to have a slogan: "Siberian money should work in Siberia, we mustn't let Moscow banks pump out our money'," Antonov said. "Now they have changed the motto, now it is: "Let Moscow banks in, let them return the money they have pumped out."
